bib.title: Compiling Agentic Workflows into LLM Weights: Near-Frontier Quality at Two Orders of Magnitude Less Cost

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Compiling Agentic Workflows into LLM Weights: Near-Frontier Quality at Two Orders of Magnitude Less Cost". Simon Dennis (i14, Univ. of Melbourne), Rivaan Patil, Kevin Shabahang, Hao Guo. Preprint, arXiv:2605.22502v1 [cs.AI], 21 May 2026 (not peer reviewed).
COVERAGE: 19 of 19 pages read (60,230 chars). Pages 1-15 and the first part of 16 were read in full, including Appendices A-C and the references. The Appendix D flowchart pages (about 17-19) are diagrams and I did not read them. I did not run the figure tool.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Same-model test: a 3B model fine-tuned on the workflow beats the same 3B base with explicit orchestration on 4 of 5 quality metrics.
 number: task success +0.18, consistency +0.22, graceful handling +0.20, naturalness +0.17, all p<0.001. Info accuracy +0.05, p=.29.
 setup: Travel booking (14 nodes), Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct, n=200 per condition, Claude Sonnet 4.5 judge. Compiled 4.11/4.75/4.34/4.07/4.12 vs. orchestrated 3.93/4.69/4.12/3.87/3.96 (task/info/consistency/graceful/natural).
 quote: "The advantage reaches significance on task success (∆ = +0.18, p <0.001), consistency (∆ = +0.22, p <0.001), graceful handling (∆ = +0.20, p <0.001), and naturalness (∆ = +0.17, p <0.001 )"
 where: p5
2. The 8B compiled model reaches 87-98% of the in-context frontier baseline, and roughly matches a LangGraph orchestrator built on Claude Sonnet 4.5.
 number: Zoom 8B vs. in-context: graceful 92%, naturalness 97%, info accuracy 87%. Insurance 8B: 4.40-4.92 vs. 4.78-5.00 (92-98%). The 3B travel model reaches only ~82% on graceful handling and naturalness.
 setup: Qwen3-8B, Zoom (14 nodes) and insurance (55 nodes, 6 hubs, 2,381 paths), n=200 each, Sonnet 4.5 judge. The in-context baseline is Sonnet 4.5 with the whole flowchart in the system prompt.
 quote: "The 8B compiled model achieves 92–98% of in-context quality on insurance claims (4.40–4.92 vs. 4.78–5.00; Table 3)"
 where: p6
3. Cost per conversation is 128-462x lower than in-context, and 77-249x lower than the LangGraph orchestrator.
 number: Travel $0.133 in-context / $0.077 LangGraph / $0.0010 compiled (128x). Zoom $0.103 / $0.054 / $0.0003 (296x). Insurance $0.327 / $0.174 / $0.0007 (462x).
 setup: Sonnet 4.5 API pricing ($3/M input, $15/M output) vs. an 8B model on a reserved A100 80GB at $2.50/hr with vLLM. Throughput comes from third-party benchmarks (Patel et al., 2024), not measured by the authors. That gives ~65x per token, times a 2-7x token-volume reduction (the compiled prompt is constant-size).
 quote: "The two factors compound:128 × cheaper for travel, 462× for insurance, with the largest advantage on the most complex procedure."
 where: p8
4. Lower failure rates than the orchestrator in travel and insurance, and comparable in Zoom. Failure means task success ≤3.
 number: Travel 5.5% vs. 24.0%. Insurance 9.0% vs. 17.0%. Zoom 11.0% vs. 9.0% (compiled 8B vs. LangGraph, so the compiled model is worse in Zoom). Travel 3B orchestrated: 4.5%.
 setup: n=200 per condition, Sonnet 4.5 judge.
 quote: "The compiled model achieves substantially lower failure rates ... than the LangGraph orchestrator in travel (5.5% vs. 24.0%) and insurance (9.0% vs. 17.0%; Table 5); Zoom rates are comparable (11.0% vs. 9.0%)."
 where: p7
5. Recompile cycle is 30-50 minutes with 8x H200 and parallel API calls. It takes 3-4 hours on a single A100.
 number: data generation 15-30 min; fine-tune 10-15 min on 8xH200 (~3 h on one A100 with 8-bit AdamW); eval spot-check 5-15 min. One-time cost $50-80 ($40 data + $10-40 compute). Break-even vs. in-context is within 500 conversations.
 setup: Estimated for ~1,600 conversations and a 12-epoch run. The 8xH200 timing is an engineering estimate, not a measured experiment.
 quote: "The fully optimized cycle (8× H200 plus parallelized API requests) completes in 30–50 minutes"
 where: p8
6. Wall-clock latency: the compiled model is faster in Zoom (29.5 s vs. 52.1 s for LangGraph) and insurance (43.2 s vs. 120.8 s, 2.8x faster than LangGraph). In travel it is slower than in-context (69.4 s vs. 55.5 s) and takes longer than the other conditions in turns (22.6 vs. ~16).
 where: p7 (Table 4)
7. Judge-robustness check: under GPT-4.1 the compiled model reaches 83-99% of in-context. The LangGraph orchestrator leads the compiled model on more metrics than under the Claude judge.
 quote: "Under GPT-4.1, the LangGraph orchestrator leads the compiled model on more metrics than under the Claude judge, particularly in travel and insurance."
 where: p16 (Appendix C)

SETUP DETAILS
- Pipeline: write the procedure as a flowchart. Sample paths and scenario variables. Have Claude Sonnet 4.5 generate turn-by-turn dialogue along each path. Run full-parameter SFT. At runtime use only a minimal system prompt such as "You are a helpful travel booking assistant". The training data contains no procedural annotations.
- Travel: 2,125 conversations (1,912 train, 213 held out). 3B bf16, one RTX 5090, AdamW 8-bit, lr 2e-5, effective batch size 16, 20 epochs (~3.5 h). Best checkpoint at epoch ~4 by held-out eval loss.
- Zoom: 8 seeds (42-49) x 783 = 6,264 training conversations. Qwen3-8B, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 on 8xA100, lr 2e-5, batch size 32, 10 epochs, best checkpoint at epoch 2.
- Insurance: 3,000 conversations (2,700 train, 300 held out). Same configuration as Zoom with 20 epochs, best checkpoint at epoch 3.
- The user simulator and the judge are both Claude Sonnet 4.5. There is a single run per condition. The paper reports no training-seed variance.

ABLATIONS
- The only ablation is 3B compiled vs. 3B orchestrated (same base model), which isolates compilation from model capacity.
- 3B to 8B scaling closes the graceful-handling and naturalness gap. This is confounded: the model family changes (Qwen 2.5 to Qwen3), data volume changes, and the domain changes.
- LoRA is only cited, not run here (Dennis et al., 2026b, an unread separate paper): "low-rank methods fail to approach full fine-tuning on procedural tasks".
- No ablation on data size, path coverage or number of epochs.

LIMITS
- Quality is measured only by LLM-as-judge on simulated users, all from Claude. Scores of 4.4-5.0 are near the ceiling. The GPT-4.1 judge compresses naturalness differences to 3.92-4.04.
- The compiled model never beats the in-context frontier baseline on any metric except travel info accuracy (3B, 4.75 vs. 4.64). It is the cheaper choice, not the better one.
- It is "competitive with" the LangGraph orchestrator rather than better. It loses on info accuracy in Zoom (4.26 vs. 4.75), where world knowledge is the bottleneck, and on graceful handling and naturalness in travel.
- The 3B-vs-LangGraph comparison is cross-run and unpaired. Only the 3B-vs-3B-orchestrated comparison is paired.
- The data is synthetic and produced by the same teacher model as the judge. There is no human evaluation and no public benchmark (no tool use, no code, no BFCL or tau-bench style tasks). All three domains are scripted customer-service dialogues.
- Cost assumes full GPU utilisation with batched vLLM, and throughput figures come from other papers. Hosting, ops, idle time and the engineering cost of building flowcharts are not counted. The break-even analysis is vague.
- The paper does not test out-of-flowchart generalisation, behaviour after a procedure change beyond retraining, or catastrophic forgetting of general ability.
- Authors are a company-affiliated group (i14) that favours the "subterranean agent" framing. The cited companion papers (Dennis et al., 2026a, 2026b) are unreleased preprints that I could not read. The "adoption barriers" framing (GitHub stars as evidence) is rhetorical.
- It is SFT/distillation only. There is no RL.

BUILDS ON: SimpleTOD (Hosseini-Asl et al., 2020); FireAct (Chen et al., 2023); SynTOD (Samarinas et al., 2024); WorkflowLLM (Fan et al., 2024); Agent Lumos (Yin et al., 2024); AgentTuning (Zeng et al., 2024); AutoTOD (Xu et al., 2024); Hsiao 2026 (procedural knowledge); Dennis et al. 2026a (in-context prompting beats orchestration) and 2026b (LoRA fails on procedures); LLM-as-judge (Zheng et al., 2023); self-preference bias (Panickssery et al., 2024); vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023).

CODE: none.

FIGURES: Fig. 1 (p3) contrasts surface orchestration, where the orchestrator sits at runtime, with the "subterranean" agent, where the orchestrator is used only to generate training data. Fig. 2 (travel flowchart) and the Appendix D flowcharts were not examined.

WHERE IT FITS: best match is generative-ai/05-RL/notes/05-post-training-for-agents.md, in "What SFT is good for", as a worked example of distilling a harness or workflow into weights. Frame it as SFT on teacher traces from a workflow, with no RL. It is evidence for "persistent structure belongs in the weights, transient state belongs in the prompt". The cost numbers and the recompile cycle are the useful teaching points. The caveats are LLM-judged quality, a single run, and synthetic scripted domains.

QUOTES (verbatim):
- p1: "persistent structure belongs in the weights, transient state belongs in the prompt."
- p2: "The orchestrator never touches the LLM at runtime. The procedure shapes the training data, and the model implicitly follows it through learned statistical regularities rather than explicit instruction."
- p9: "The quality gap to a frontier model is small (2–13%)"

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The text extracted cleanly. Page numbers are PDF pages. The Appendix D flowchart pages are image-only, so no text came from them. The reference list prints some 2025 arXiv papers as 2026 (for example Cemri, Zhu, Hsiao).
